# Evaluation of Open Primaries as the Most Effective Method of Selecting Candidates for Elections

## Introduction
This report evaluates the claim that open primaries are the most effective method of selecting candidates for elections. The analysis is based on four distinct sources, each providing unique insights into the effectiveness of open primaries compared to other methods.

## Open Primaries and Voter Choice
Open primaries allow all registered voters, regardless of party affiliation, to participate in the primary election process. This method can lead to a more considered choice between candidates and parties, as voters are not limited by party lines. In safe districts, where voters typically choose from members of the same party, open primaries enable voters to select the next representative based on their past record and views on significant issues, thereby bringing ideological differences within parties under closer examination [1].

## Centrism and Political Discourse
One of the key benefits of open primaries is the potential to elect more centrist candidates for the general election. By allowing all voters to participate, open primaries can prevent the dominance of overly ideological candidates who might alienate moderate voters necessary for winning elections. This moderation can foster a more consensual political atmosphere, focusing debates on core issues rather than extreme positions. Candidates elected through open primaries are more likely to be willing to compromise across the aisle, which can help alleviate political gridlock [2].

## Manipulation and Unintended Outcomes
However, open primaries are not without their drawbacks. The lack of party affiliation restrictions can make internal elections susceptible to manipulation by those hostile to the party's aims. This can result in the election of "unelectable" candidates who may not represent the true interests of the party or the electorate. Such outcomes can damage the political process and undermine public trust in the electoral system [3].

## Addressing Disenfranchisement
Open primaries can also address the issue of disenfranchisement in majoritarian simple plurality electoral systems, where only two major parties often dominate. By allowing voters to support candidates of a major party that align more closely with their political views, open primaries can give more people the opportunity to influence the election outcome. This inclusivity can lead to the emergence of serious third-party candidates who pass the primary test, thereby enriching the political landscape [4].

## Conclusion
The effectiveness of open primaries in selecting candidates for elections is a complex issue. While they offer benefits such as fostering centrist politics and addressing voter disenfranchisement, they also present risks of manipulation and unintended outcomes. Therefore, the claim that open primaries are the most effective method is supported in some aspects but undermined in others. The overall effectiveness may depend on the specific context and the mechanisms in place to mitigate potential drawbacks.

1. Open Primaries allow for the electorate to make a considered choice between candidate and party, with other considerations beyond the partisan being up for consideration. In safe districts, voters are given a choice between members of the same party, allowing for voters to effectively choose the next member based upon past record and views on big issues, allowing for the ideological cleavages within parties to be brought under closer examination, with voters in the safe seat choosing the type of Conservatism/Liberalism/Socialism they prefer. [2]

We have seen instances where ‘unelectable’ candidates have been elected by Open Primary as means of discrediting a party and helping their opponents win the general election. A famous instance of this was in the Democratic Primary for the US Senate seat in South Carolina, where the winner, Alvin Greene became the candidate with little advertising or successful fundraising, leading to accusations of a Republican campaign to make re-election of their incumbent, Jim DeMint, much easier. Open Primaries counters this by allowing these voters a chance to vote for candidates of a major party that are closer to their own political persuasion, thus giving as many people as possible the opportunity to register their opinion on who will be their representative for the next term, ending disillusionment with predictable election results.
